title: A Conversation with John Sailer: How to Make Universities More Accountable
author: Restoring the West
summary: Restoring the West interviews John D. Sailer, director of higher education policy at the Manhattan Institute, about model legislation designed to restore accountability in university governance. Sailer explains that governing boards have historically had oversight authority but have allowed it to atrophy through excessive deference to scholars and administrators. He argues that ideological capture in higher education wasn't produced by top-down legislation and can't be fixed by legislation alone — it requires good personnel engaging directly in the details of hiring and curriculum decisions. Critics who worry the bill undermines academic freedom misunderstand it: the legislation adds the board as a new check without dictating what goes into individual classes. The core curriculum question — what a well-educated person looks like — is not a matter of disciplinary expertise but of institutional vision, and boards have both the standing and the obligation to answer it.
points: Governing boards have long had the authority to oversee curriculum and hiring but have allowed it to atrophy — new model legislation from the Manhattan Institute would require them to exercise that authority actively.

Ideological capture in higher education was not produced by top-down policy, and policy alone cannot fix it: reform is ultimately about personnel and about good people getting into the details of hiring and curricular decisions.

The legislation does not undermine shared governance — it makes governance truly shared by adding the board to the existing checks and balances without giving boards authority over what happens inside individual classes.
The core curriculum question — what a well-educated person looks like — is not a matter of disciplinary expertise but of institutional vision, which is exactly what governing boards exist to define.
If universities do not take governance reform seriously, the trajectory is less confidence, more alienation, and eventually less public funding — for their own sake they must start listening.
quotes: Public universities have a responsibility not only to seek the truth, but to prepare students to flourish in their careers and assume the responsibilities of citizenship. Too often, they failed to do so.

It wasn't top-down legislation that brought us to this point. And legislation alone certainly won't fix the problem. Often, reform is about personnel, and it's about good personnel getting in the weeds.
our legislation does not do away with shared governance. If anything, it makes governance truly shared, adding the board to the list of checks and balances.
the question of what should and shouldn’t be in a core isn’t a matter of disciplinary expertise. It’s about a university’s vision, its understanding of what a well-educated person looks like.

the result will be that fewer deans and associate provosts will see themselves as the internal resistance. These are the ones responsible for allocating faculty lines and overseeing hundreds of curricular decisions.

For their own sake, universities should take seriously the concern that higher education has become detached from the public it’s supposed to serve. If they want to survive, they have to start listening.
